talks.title: BSidesCharm 2022 Closing Keynote - Secure the Era
talks.teaser: Evaluates BSidesCharm 2022 Closing Keynote - Secure the Era and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Mick Baccio, former White House threat intelligence branch chief and Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) for Pete Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential campaign ("Pete for America"), reflects on the unique, high-stakes operational realities of securing a national political campaign. In this BSidesCharm 2022 keynote, Baccio describes presidential campaigns as fast-paced, temporary startups that scale from zero to hundreds of staff members within months, operating under extreme public scrutiny and nation-state threat pressures without traditional enterprise IT foundations or compliance mandates. He details pragmatic security architectures, threat modeling across distinct campaign pillars, third-party SaaS dependencies, and external perimeter defense.

Key Topics:
- Threat modeling political campaigns: "Principal Ops" ring-zero executive protection vs. policy, finance, and voter data assets
- Operational constraints and culture: training young, non-technical staffers on essential security hygiene (MFA) without stalling campaign momentum
- Third-party SaaS supply chain risks: reliance on shared political database ecosystems (ActBlue, NGP VAN, Civis Analytics)
- External perimeter threats and digital gamesmanship: domain typosquatting (dnstwist), domain redirection hijacking, and physical mail screening operations

Technical Details:
Baccio explains that a presidential campaign functions as an incorporation with an 18-month lifespan, funded entirely by donor contributions where every dollar allocated to security represents a dollar diverted from advertising or field organizing in critical primary states like Iowa. Without regulatory frameworks (such as FISMA or commercial compliance scorecards) enforcing security standards, CISOs must build security cultures from scratch. Campaign personnel are predominantly young, recent college graduates with little security awareness, making simple, non-intrusive hygiene—most notably universal multi-factor authentication (MFA)—the primary defense against repeat incidents of the 2016 DNC and Podesta phishing compromises.

The operational threat model is structured around core campaign pillars. "Principal Ops" (the candidate, spouse, family, and traveling leadership) demands hardened ring-zero protections and VIP executive security. "Policy Ops" requires safeguards against intellectual property theft by state-sponsored actors seeking advance insight into policy platforms and debate preparation. Meanwhile, campaign data operations rely almost entirely on an external SaaS ecosystem. Political campaigns depend on centralized vendor platforms such as ActBlue (donation processing), NGP VAN (voter tracking and CRM), and Civis Analytics. These platforms represent critical supply-chain dependencies where upstream data breaches or unauthorized access (such as past incidents where rival campaigns accessed opposing voter files) can inflict catastrophic operational harm.

On the external perimeter, Baccio highlights domain security and political gamesmanship. Running dnstwist against peteforamerica.com uncovered over 525 lookalike and typosquatted domains that required continuous monitoring and rapid registrar takedowns to prevent phishing. Political adversaries routinely weaponized domain registrations: third parties registered petebuttigieg.org to redirect visitors to Donald Trump’s official campaign website, while others bought misspoken candidate URLs during televised debates (such as redirecting Joe 30330 to competing campaigns). Furthermore, the physical threat environment demanded improvised operational security, including establishing isolated off-site mail screening facilities equipped with dedicated ventilation systems to inspect physical correspondence for hazardous substances or explosive devices.

Key Takeaways:
Securing temporary, high-threat organizations requires prioritizing practical, low-friction controls—such as universal multi-factor authentication and password managers—that protect users without hindering organizational velocity. CISOs must account for the systemic supply-chain risks introduced by shared SaaS data brokers (NGP VAN, ActBlue), auditing permissions and monitoring session anomalies. Finally, the political ecosystem must transcend partisan competition to establish cross-campaign threat intelligence sharing channels, ensuring indicators of compromise and phishing campaigns are collaboratively defended against common nation-state adversaries.

talks.title: BSidesCharm 2022 - The Uncensorable Stack: Malicious Applications of Blockchain Tech
talks.teaser: Details BSidesCharm 2022 - The Uncensorable Stack: Malicious Applications of Blockchain Tech and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Observed Criminal Uses

A BSides Charm talk surveys malicious blockchain applications, beginning with CTI-documented cases: cryptojacking infected hosts to mine privacy coins like Monero, and crypto-clipping malware swaps wallet addresses copied to the clipboard. North Korean APT campaigns also distribute trojanized cryptocurrency trading apps built with Electron to steal private keys.

Blockchain Properties for Attackers

The speaker explains how decentralization, immutability, and censorship resistance benefit adversaries seeking infrastructure that survives takedowns—contrasting with centralized hosting or bulletproof providers that authorities can pressure.

The Uncensorable Stack Concept

He outlines a theoretical architecture combining blockchains for DNS, compute, and storage into a user-friendly uncensorable application. Integrating these layers could give operators strong guarantees against conventional disruption.

Emerging C2 Techniques

Research papers proposed hiding command-and-control in Bitcoin script opcodes; the talk notes APT groups have since implemented similar ideas in the wild. Smart-contract flexibility and limited auditing tooling, he warns, create ongoing opportunities for abuse beyond financial crime alone.

talks.title: BSidesCharm 2022 - Forecasting Cyber Attacks
talks.teaser: Demonstrates BSidesCharm 2022 - Forecasting Cyber Attacks and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Forecasting goal

Charlene Dever Vásquez presents probabilistic risk modeling for cyber, using MITRE ATT&CK scenarios to estimate attack probability and give organizations time to build mitigations. She offers a downloadable model from the talk.

Core forecasting idea

You can start with little data: broad probability ranges stay accurate while narrow ranges require more information. Models are not crystal balls—they depend on inputs—but reliably output event probabilities and counts.

Key terms and methods

She defines threat as weakness/vulnerability and likelihood as chance an actor can exploit it; eliminating either removes risk. Three main methods: iterative Bayesian joint probability (Venn-diagram overlap), Monte Carlo simulation (random samples within best/worst bounds producing a distribution), and a third newer model previewed at the end.

talks.title: BSidesCharm 2022 - Into the Breach: An Analysis of State Political Party Account Exposure
talks.teaser: Examines BSidesCharm 2022 - Into the Breach: An Analysis of State Political Party Account Exposure and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Election exposure research

Andrew from DoD presents analysis of U.S. state political party websites exposing private email addresses for volunteers, county chairs, and staff. He connects public contact lists to credential reuse and phishing risk in election-adjacent organizations with minimal security staffing.

Systemic data breach overlap

Scanning roughly 9,900 published addresses, about two-thirds appeared in prior breach corpora—suggesting parties lack situational awareness of compromised accounts. Exposure mixes personal Gmail and Yahoo accounts with organizational .gov and party-domain emails.

Why published emails matter

Email remains a trusted authentication and communication key; publishing addresses aids outreach but expands spear-phishing and account takeover surfaces. The research argues down-ballot political infrastructure needs the same credential hygiene and breach monitoring expected in enterprise security programs.
